name.en: Sanuki (Temples 65-88, and the return to Temple 1)

description.en: The last of the four dōjō, and the one that closes the circuit: Temple 65 Sankaku-ji to Temple 88 Ōkubo-ji, then on to Temple 1 Ryōzen-ji where the pilgrimage began — 202.2 km along 24 temple-to-temple henro trail relations. The temples stand closest together here — Temple 68 to Temple 69 is 0.11 km and Temple 72 to Temple 73 is 0.46 km. The last relation is the 39.8 km return from Ōkubo-ji to Ryōzen-ji, and it is the only leg in this section longer than 30 km. Sanuki carries the fourth of the four stages of spiritual progression the pilgrimage maps onto Shikoku's four provinces: nirvana.

distanceNote.en: 202.2 km is this section's own walked line — the shortest connected path through its 24 pinned henro trail relations, measured with the repository's own way graph. Its member ways sum to 203.4 km; the difference is the spurs a walked line leaves out. The four dōjō together measure 1,140.9 km, against the pilgrimage's traditional ~1,200 km figure. Modern walked totals range from about 1,140 km (most efficient) to about 1,400 km (with all variant paths).

estimatedDays.note: Derived from this section's 202.2 km at the pace the whole pilgrimage's own declared figures imply — 1,200 km in 30 to 60 days, typically 45, so 20 to 40 km a day and typically 26.7. min and max are rounded up, typical to the nearest day. The four sections come to 31 to 59 days, typically 44.

elevationRange.maxMetersNote: Temple 66 Unpen-ji, at 911 m, stands in this section and is the highest temple on the whole circuit. Pilgrims anywhere on the circuit may cross higher mountain passes between temples (especially in the Iya/Mt. Tsurugi region of Tokushima), but no temple is above 950 m. No ascent or descent total is declared: the ten-stage figures this section replaces were summed over stages that no longer exist, and per-section totals wait on the walked line.

origin.en: The pilgrimage traces the path of the monk Kūkai (774-835), founder of Shingon Buddhism in Japan. Kūkai practiced asceticism across Shikoku before founding the monastic center at Mount Kōya. The 88-temple circuit was formalized during the Edo period (1603-1868). The phrase 'Dōgyō Ninin' (walking with two) inscribed on the pilgrim's hat signifies that Kōbō Daishi walks with every pilgrim.

description.en: A calligraphy book purchased at Temple 1 (2,000-3,500 JPY). At each temple, monks write the temple name, principal deity, and temple number in calligraphy and apply three red stamps. Cost: 500 JPY per temple (44,000 JPY total). Stamp hours: 7:00-17:00. One book is carried across all four dōjō.
'Walking with Two' — the belief that Kōbō Daishi walks alongside every pilgrim. Inscribed on the sedge hat. The pilgrim is never alone.

Traditional pilgrim outfit: white jacket (hakui, 白衣) symbolizing purity and readiness for death, sedge hat (sugegasa), walking staff (kongōzue) representing Kōbō Daishi himself, stole (wagesa), prayer beads (juzu), and name slips (osamefuda) deposited at each temple.

At each temple: bow at the gate, purify at the water basin, ring the bell, offer incense and candle at the Main Hall, chant the Heart Sutra (Hannya Shingyō), repeat at the Daishi Hall, receive the stamp. The full sequence takes 20-30 minutes per temple.

Charitable gifts from locals to pilgrims — food, drinks, money, or lodging. A deeply rooted tradition in Shikoku. It is customary to accept osettai graciously and give a name slip (osamefuda) in return.

The walking staff is considered an embodiment of Kōbō Daishi. It must be washed and placed in the room before the pilgrim washes. It must never be placed on the ground where it could be stepped over. In historical times, if a pilgrim died, the staff was used as their grave marker.

etiquette.en: Remove shoes before entering temple buildings.
Do not ring the bell when leaving a temple — only upon arrival.
The walking staff must never be used to point or gesture.
Accept osettai graciously, even if you do not need it. Refusing is considered disrespectful to Kōbō Daishi.

relevance.en: The definitive English-language book on the Shikoku pilgrimage. Statler walked the route multiple times and documented its history, culture, and personal meaning.
Translations of Kūkai's major philosophical and religious writings. Essential for understanding the spiritual foundation of the pilgrimage.

description.en: Celebrated at Temple 75 (Zentsū-ji), Kūkai's birthplace, which stands in this section. Special ceremonies and increased pilgrim activity.

historicalSignificance.en: The Shikoku pilgrimage is one of the few circular pilgrimages in the world and the most important Buddhist pilgrimage in Japan. It embodies the Shingon Buddhist concept of spiritual progression through four stages: awakening, discipline, enlightenment, and nirvana — mapped onto the four provinces of Shikoku.

notes.en: Open year-round but rainy season (June-July) and typhoon season (August-September) are challenging. Winter walking is possible but some mountain temples may be difficult to access. Peak seasons are spring (cherry blossoms) and autumn (fall foliage).

accommodationNotes.en: Shukubo (temple lodging): 6,000-8,500 JPY with meals. Minshuku: 5,500-7,500 JPY with meals. Business hotels: 3,000-8,000 JPY without meals. Cash is essential — credit cards rarely accepted at traditional lodging. Advance reservations recommended.

cellularNotes.en: Good coverage in towns and along main roads. Weak or no signal on mountain trails.

waterNotes.en: Vending machines are ubiquitous in Japan, even in rural areas.

notes.en: Nearest airport to Temple 1, where this section's closing return ends. Bus to Naruto/Bando area.
Trains circle most of Shikoku. Useful for reaching temples or skipping difficult sections. JR passes available.

sources.notes: The day divisions are cut by rule rather than taken from a guidebook, so they can be re-run. The rule: a day ends at a temple whenever one falls between 25 and 30 km along this section's route.main.geojson; where no temple does, it ends at the nearest named accommodation or town waypoint on the line instead. Two tie-breaks make it deterministic. Where several candidates qualify the day ends at the one nearest 27.5 km, the middle of the band, and where two are equally near, at the earlier one along the line — the same test in both arms. The fallback arm is not confined to the band, because it exists for the stretches where the band is empty. It is confined to places strictly ahead of the previous day's end, and that clause is what keeps the cut advancing: without it the arm can re-select the day's own starting place, and in shikoku-88-sanuki it does — from Sakaide at 82.48 km the target is 109.98 km, Sakaide sits exactly 27.5 km from it and the next candidate 32.11 km, so the day ends where it began and the cut deadlocks. "Named" means the waypoint carries a name that is a non-empty string other than the literal "Unnamed" the enrichment writes when OpenStreetMap gave the node none: accommodation is not one of the types enrichment requires a name for, so two unnamed accommodation waypoints sit in this pilgrimage's files and the rule filters them itself. A candidate counts as on the line when it lies within 500 m of it, the radius build-ways snaps a stage boundary across. A temple means a waypoint carrying a templeNumber, which is also the field that says which temple it is. The word has a looser reading these files admit and this rule refuses: 163 of their sacred_site waypoints carry subtype church and 47 subtype wayside_shrine, one of the churches named "27 Kōnomine-ji" and standing 52 m from Temple 27's own waypoint. Read that way the cut still yields 40 stages and still looks plausible — it moves 15 of the 40 day ends and puts 23 days inside the band instead of 18 — and nothing errors, which is why the definition belongs in the rule and not in a note beside it. Position along the line is measured by perpendicular projection onto route.main.geojson, not read from a waypoint's own kmFromStart, which this pilgrimage records on two different scales. Section boundaries override both arms, and the override has a stated trigger: when the section's end anchor lies no more than 30 km ahead of the current day's start, the day ends there whatever its length, and neither arm is consulted. Without that threshold the arms run to exhaustion and split a last short day off against the boundary — the four sections come to 42 stages rather than 40, one of the two extras a 0.41 km walk from Guest House Sakura-an to Yakuō-ji. shikoku-88-sanuki holds Ōkubo-ji (Temple 88) fixed under that same 30 km trigger, and separately walks the closing return from it to Temple 1 as one stage. Those are two clauses and not one: drop the hold and that day runs 190 m further to Minshuku Yasokubo, leaving the return with no day-end at all; keep the hold and drop the one-stage rule and the fallback emits a 0.19 km day to that same lodging, the only named place on the line past Ōkubo-ji. The spec's original rule was temples only, and the temple spacing does not carry it. Of the 88 temple-to-temple legs, measured on these same lines, only 4 fall inside 25-30 km, while 10 exceed 30 km and carry 552.3 km — 48% of the 1,140.9 km circuit — the longest Temple 37 to Temple 38 at 82.7 km. Across those ten there is no temple to end a day at in either direction, which is what the second arm is for; without it half the route could not be paced at all. Cut 2026-09-09 against the walked line measured the same day. This section came to 6 stages, the four dojo to 40. The rule's realised range runs from 13.05 km to 59.61 km, and two days sit far outside the band it aims at: shikoku-88-awa's stage 3, Ido-ji (Temple 17) to GuestHouse & Cafe Green House, at 52.9 km, and this section's stage 3, Sakaide to Sanuki, at 59.6 km. Neither is a fault in the enrichment — every named accommodation and town waypoint in both sections already lies within 300 m of the walked line, so the on-the-line test excludes none of them — both are the rule meeting OpenStreetMap's lodging coverage, which after Ido-ji offers Awa nothing for 52.94 km and after Sakaide offers Sanuki nothing for 59.61 km. No maximum refuses a day that long, because refusing would leave those stretches with no day-end at all; each of the two stages carries the fact as a stage warning instead. Each stage's distanceKm is the length of route.main.geojson between its own two anchors, rounded to one decimal, and each anchor's own note records which arm chose it. Every waypoint's stageIndex and kmFromStart is derived from the same line and the same boundaries as the cut above. A waypoint belongs to the stage whose stretch of route.main.geojson contains the perpendicular projection of its coordinate, and its kmFromStart is where that projection falls along this section's line, in km from the section's start anchor, rounded to one decimal. Both are section-local. Neither is read from the file's own order, which still runs by the values the old ten-stage cut left and which nothing downstream consults: build-ways sorts a stage's moments and marks by their position along that stage, and reversing the feature order leaves every ways/ file byte-identical. The stretches are the ones build-ways cuts — each stage anchor snapped to its nearest vertex of the line, searched forward of the anchor before it. All 44 boundaries across the four sections snapped, each section's first to vertex 0 and its last to the final vertex, so the stretches tile every line end to end and no waypoint can project outside them; none does. Re-assigned 2026-09-09 over the old ten-stage cut's values, under which every enriched waypoint in all four sections read stageIndex 0 and every temple carried a kmFromStart on one scale running around the whole circuit — 0-149.8 km in Awa, 225.2-557.8 in Tosa, 583.6-919.0 in Iyo, 938.3-1080.5 in Sanuki — rather than the section-local scale of the enriched waypoints beside them. In this section 361 of 389 waypoints changed stage and 388 changed kmFromStart. One consequence is recorded rather than smoothed: a day-end place projects within metres of the vertex its own boundary snapped to and can land either side of it, and 12 of the four sections' 36 mid-route day-ends land past theirs — by 20.9 m at the widest, and by a floating-point residual at Kanjizai-ji (Temple 40), which projects onto its boundary vertex exactly — so those are filed on the day that begins there rather than the day that ends there. No package turns on it: build-ways writes a stage's own start and end place as moments whatever their stageIndex, and a moment within 150 m of either never counts toward the coverage bar.

osm.note: 24 relations, 65番札所~66番札所 through 87番札所~88番札所 plus 13766029, 四国遍路 88番札所大窪寺~1番札所霊山寺 — the 39.84 km closing return to Temple 1 that makes the pilgrimage circular. In walking order. The Overpass query above is pilgrimage-wide and returns all 89 四国遍路 relations; each section pins the slice of that result it walks. A boundary relation belongs to the section that walks it, so Sanuki begins at Temple 65, where shikoku-88-iyo's last relation ends.
